duomo: The Gothic cathedral of pink and white marble, with 135 spires and over three thousand statues, topped by the golden Madonnina. Inside you walk among columns as tall as trees; outside you climb onto the rooftop terraces, among the spires, with views over the square and, on clear days, the Alps.
galleria: "Milan's drawing room": a 19th-century glass-and-iron arcade with mosaic floors, historic shops and cafés. On the bull mosaic in the centre, spin on your heel for luck.
scala: In front of Italy's most famous opera house is the square with the Leonardo monument. The museum, in the same building, has costumes, instruments, scores and mementos of Verdi, Toscanini and Callas; from a box you can look into the auditorium when there are no rehearsals.
novecento: Museo del Novecento and Piazza Duomo

The museum of 20th-century Italian art, in the Arengario on Piazza Duomo: Pellizza da Volpedo's "Fourth Estate", the Futurists (Boccioni, Balla) and Fontana. The big windows look onto the square and the Cathedral from an unusual angle.
quadrilatero: Via Montenapoleone, Via della Spiga, Via Sant'Andrea and Via Manzoni: the streets of the great fashion houses, with neoclassical palazzi, hidden courtyards and shop windows that only cost you a look. Behind Via Manzoni is the Bagatti Valsecchi Museum.
castello: The fortress of the Dukes of Milan, with the Filarete Tower over the moat and courtyards that form the heart of the city. Inside are the civic museums (including Michelangelo's last sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà). Behind the castle lies Parco Sempione, stretching to the Arco della Pace.
cenacolo: In the refectory of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper in 1495–98. The visit lasts 15 minutes, in groups of up to 40, in climate-controlled air to protect the painting. Next door is the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie, with its cloister.
brera: The artists' quarter: cobbled streets, workshops, galleries and bars around the Academy and the Pinacoteca. In Via Fiori Chiari and around, on the third Sunday of the month (except August), there's an antiques market.
pinacoteca: The great collection of Italian painting, in a 17th-century palazzo: Hayez's "The Kiss", Mantegna's Dead Christ, Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin, Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus and Piero della Francesca's Brera Altarpiece.
santambrogio: The basilica of Milan's patron saint, founded by Ambrose in the 4th century and rebuilt in Romanesque style: the arcaded atrium, the church with its 9th-century golden altar and the apse mosaics. Outside is the Devil's Column, with two holes: tradition says they're the marks of his horns.
colonne: Sixteen Roman columns from the 2nd–3rd century, in front of the basilica of San Lorenzo: Milan's most important Roman monument. In the evening the space in front of the columns is a meeting place for young people and students.
navigli: The canals of the Naviglio Grande and the Darsena, once Milan's port: tenement houses with iron balconies, workshops and bars on the water. In the evening, from aperitivo time on, it's the liveliest area of the city.
portanuova: Porta Nuova: Bosco Verticale and Piazza Gae Aulenti

Modern Milan: the circular Piazza Gae Aulenti at the foot of the UniCredit Tower, the glass skyscrapers and, a little further on, the Bosco Verticale, the two towers with twenty-one thousand plants on their balconies.
